title: Specialised Agencies and UN Reform

cards.h: The working arms of the UN, and how to fix the whole
cards.b:
Most of what the UN does day to day is done not by the Security Council but by its specialised agencies, funds and programmes: vaccines, food aid, air safety, labour standards, telecom frequencies, weather data.

At the same time, the UN is under pressure to reform: its Council reflects 1945, its finances are in crisis, and in 2025 the Secretary-General launched the UN80 Initiative to cut and merge.

UPSC asks: what are the specialised agencies and how do they work? What reforms are needed, especially of the Security Council? What is India's case for a permanent seat? This lesson covers both halves. Link the agencies to Mitrany's functionalism, which they embody.

Under Articles 57 and 63 of the Charter, specialised agencies are autonomous international organisations linked to the UN by agreements with ECOSOC. They have their own members, budgets, governing bodies and heads.

They differ from funds and programmes (UNICEF, UNDP, WFP, UNHCR), which are subsidiary bodies of the UN, mostly funded by voluntary donations.

The idea comes from functionalism: David Mitrany's A Working Peace System (1943) argued that cooperation on technical tasks would build peace. Some agencies are older than the UN: the ITU (1865), the Universal Postal Union (1874) and the ILO (1919).

There are 15 specialised agencies, plus related bodies such as the IAEA and the WTO, which report to the UN but are not specialised agencies.

Examples of their work: WHO declared smallpox eradicated (1980) and coordinated COVID-19 (declared a pandemic in March 2020). The ILO is tripartite, with governments, employers and workers. ICAO sets aviation rules; ITU assigns radio spectrum and satellite slots.

Headquarters: WHO, ILO, ITU, WIPO and WMO in Geneva; FAO and IFAD in Rome; UNESCO in Paris; ICAO in Montreal; IMO in London; UPU in Bern; IMF and World Bank in Washington.

cards.h: Strengths and problems of the agencies
cards.b:
Strengths

Technical expertise, global standards, near-universal membership, effective in non-political fields (aviation, post, health data).

Problems

  • Politicisation. The US left UNESCO in 1984, rejoined in 2003, left in 2018 after Palestine's admission (2011), rejoined in 2023, and announced withdrawal again in 2025.
  • Funding. Most money is voluntary and earmarked by donors, which distorts priorities. WHO's budget depended heavily on a few donors and foundations.
  • US exit from WHO, effective January 2026, cut a major funder.
  • Overlap. Many bodies work on the same issues (food, health, gender).
  • Great-power rivalry for top posts, such as China's campaigns for agency heads.

The WHO Pandemic Agreement (adopted May 2025) showed that agencies can still make new rules, even without the US.

• Security Council reflects 1945: no permanent seat for Africa, Latin America or India; Europe is over-represented.
  • The veto blocks action on mass atrocities and on conflicts involving the P5.
  • Finances. Late or unpaid dues, and overdependence on a few donors.
  • Bureaucracy. Too many mandates and overlapping bodies.
  • Effectiveness. Slow response to crises.
  • Representation of non-state actors and of future generations.

Reform history: the Council's 1965 enlargement; Kofi Annan's In Larger Freedom (2005), which led to the Human Rights Council and Peacebuilding Commission (2005-06); Ban's and Guterres's management reforms (2019 development system reform); the Pact for the Future (September 2024); and UN80 (2025).

Talks are held in the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) of the General Assembly, since 2009. Any change needs a Charter amendment under Article 108: two-thirds of the Assembly, then ratification by two-thirds of members including all five P5.

Main groups

  • G4 (Brazil, Germany, India, Japan): new permanent and non-permanent seats, and a 15-year review of the veto for new members.
  • Uniting for Consensus ("Coffee Club", led by Italy, Pakistan, Argentina, South Korea and others): no new permanent seats, more long-term elected seats.
  • African Union (Ezulwini Consensus, 2005): two permanent seats with veto and five non-permanent seats for Africa.
  • L.69 group of developing countries supports expansion in both categories.

The P5 differ: the US, UK, France and Russia have voiced support for India's bid in principle; China is opposed or silent. Veto restraint: the France-Mexico initiative and the ACT code of conduct on atrocities.

Guterres launched UN80 in March 2025, amid a cash crunch caused largely by US cuts.

  • Efficiency: cut posts and costs; move staff from high-cost cities (New York, Geneva) to cheaper hubs such as Nairobi and Bonn. For 2026, posts were cut and the regular budget trimmed to about $3.7 billion.
  • Mandate review: the General Assembly is reviewing tens of thousands of mandates for overlap.
  • Structural change: proposals include merging UNDP with UNOPS, merging UNFPA with UN Women, and phasing out UNAIDS. The UNFPA-UN Women idea is controversial; women's groups fear loss of focus.

Critics say UN80 is cost-cutting driven by donors, not a vision. Supporters say slimming is the only way to survive. The new Secretary-General, from January 2027, will carry it forward.

• The P5 veto over reform itself (Article 108).
  • Regional rivalries. Pakistan opposes India, Italy opposes Germany, Argentina and Mexico oppose Brazil, China opposes Japan.
  • Africa's unity on Ezulwini makes compromise difficult.
  • Efficiency versus representation. A bigger Council may be fairer but slower.
  • Money talks. Donors shape agencies through earmarked funds.
  • US ambivalence. A US that is leaving bodies has little interest in strengthening them.

Thinkers' views: realists expect no reform without a shift in power; liberals favour incremental change (working methods, veto restraint); Global South scholars see legitimacy as the core issue.

• Case for a permanent seat: the world's most populous country (since 2023), a large economy, a founding member, one of the largest peacekeeping contributors, nuclear restraint, and a voice of the Global South. Elected eight times as a non-permanent member, most recently 2021-22; candidate for 2028-29.
  • Diplomacy: works in the G4 and the L.69 group, and supports the African position; calls for text-based negotiations in the IGN.
  • Agencies: active in WHO (vaccines; "pharmacy of the world"), ILO, FAO (International Year of Millets 2023), ITU (hosted the World Telecommunication Standardization Assembly in New Delhi, 2024), and the International Solar Alliance as a new treaty body.
  • Criticisms India faces: its record on certain human rights resolutions and its reluctance to support R2P.

Structure: define agencies (Articles 57, 63; functionalism), list key ones with roles, give strengths and problems (politicisation, funding, US exits). Then reform: why needed, history (2005, 2024 Pact), Council models (G4, UfC, Ezulwini, L.69), Article 108 hurdle, UN80. End with India's case and a way forward.

quiz.q: Specialised agencies are linked to the UN through agreements under Articles:
quiz.w: Article 57 on agencies and Article 63 on ECOSOC agreements.
The ITU dates from 1865; the UPU from 1874; the ILO from 1919.

quiz.q: The ILO's structure is distinctive because it is:
quiz.w: Governments, employers and workers all vote.
The IMO is in London; FAO in Rome.

quiz.q: Security Council reform requires amendment under Article:
quiz.w: Two-thirds of the Assembly and two-thirds ratification including all P5.

quiz.q: Which group opposes new permanent seats?
quiz.w: Led by Italy, Pakistan and others.

quiz.q: The Ezulwini Consensus (2005) is the position of:
quiz.w: Two permanent seats with veto and five non-permanent seats for Africa.

quiz.q: Kofi Annan's 2005 reform report was titled:
quiz.w: It led to the Human Rights Council and Peacebuilding Commission.

quiz.q: Among UN80 proposals is a merger of:
quiz.w: Along with UNDP-UNOPS and phasing out UNAIDS.
